newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Surprise NZ jobs data shouldn't stall easing.
newsitem.headline: Surprise NZ jobs data shouldn't stall easing.

text.p: New Zealand recorded its lowest unemployment rate in more than eight years on Tuesday but economists said an equally unexpected decline in employment growth left the door ajar for a further monetary policy easing.
Statistics New Zealand said the seasonally adjusted unemployment rate dropped to 5.9 percent in the December quarter, its lowest level since June, 1988.
Prime minister Jim Bolger hailed the news as "tremendously positive", saying European politicians would give their right arm for such a low unemployment rate.
While the fall in unemployment took financial markets by surprise, even more perplexing was negative employment growth of 0.5 percent for the quarter.
Economists polled by Reuters had forecast 0.325 percent employment growth for the quarter with an unemployment rate of 6.42 percent.

"Certainly a somewhat surprising result," said Paul Stewart, chief economist at ANZ bank. "The weaker employment growth overall was to be expected, but some confusing signals in terms of participation and the unemployment levels."

Economists noted that the seasonally adjusted participation rate had fallen almost a full percentage point to 65.5 percent from 66.4 percent in the September quarter, which could explain the low unemployment rate.
But at first glance, the numbers didn't appear to tally with the fall-off in employment growth.
"First instinct is to think that the numbers are wrong," said BNZ economist Peter Jolly. "We're going to have to dig a bit further into exactly what went on there."

Statistics New Zealand said a change in the unemployment benefit structure allowing beneficiaries to earn more income within a three-month period was one factor in the unseasonal drop in unemployment.
Benefit changes which came into effect on July 1 allow single parents to earn more money before their Domestic Purposes Benefit abates, and more had entered the work force as a result.
Employment growth of 0.8 percent in the September quarter was primarily driven by a spike in part-time employment, but part-time employment fell 5.0 percent in the December quarter.

Government Statistician Len Cook suggested fewer women would be able to work in the December quarter because of school holidays and said it was the September quarter which had really recorded the interesting change.
"The December quarter...has really returned to the long-run average of the last five years," he said.
Financial markets failed to move on the data, a small rise in the currency the only discernable reaction, but economists said the numbers were mildly positive for the inflation outlook.
Despite the conflicting nature of the statistics, they augered well for a monetary policy easing.

"It confirms that the economy was very weak towards the end of the last year. I would think the economy was a little weaker than also the Reserve Bank had expected and that is probably good news for the inflation prospects," said Deutsche Morgan Grenfell Bank Chief Economist Ulf Schoefisch.
"Looking further ahead I think there is scope for some mild further easing by the (Reserve) bank," he said.
While the bank would undoubtedly mull over the mixed results before the release of its Economic Projections on March 13, the fall in employment growth was heartening.
The markets would now look to wages data due later this month -- the December Labour Cost Index and Quarterly Employment Survey -- as indicator of whether an easing was on the agenda.
